input: This pricing case considers a SaaS tier and examines the volume at which the tier breaks even. The price of the tier is $377 per unit, while the variable cost is $197 per unit, which means that each unit sold contributes 180 towards covering the fixed costs. The fixed costs amount to $221k per year. Based on these figures, the break-even volume works out at 1228 units per year. The current volume, by comparison, stands at 6863 units per year, which is comfortably above the break-even level, indicating that the tier currently covers its fixed costs with a considerable margin to spare. In other words, the contribution generated by the current level of sales exceeds the fixed cost base by a wide margin, and the tier would remain above its break-even point even if the volume achieved were to fall substantially from its present level, provided that the price and the cost figures themselves remained unchanged. This kind of analysis is commonly used as a first screen when a pricing decision is being considered, since it identifies the volume below which the tier would begin to make a loss at the stated price. It is worth noting, however, that the volume figures used in this analysis are last year's actuals, and the effect of the price on the volume that can be sold has not been estimated, so the analysis does not indicate how the position would change if the price itself were altered. A fuller treatment would require some estimate of that response, together with an assessment of how the fixed cost base might itself change if volumes were to grow or contract significantly.
target: The SaaS tier stands well above its break-even volume: break-even is 1228 units per year and current volume is 6863 units per year. The price is $377 per unit and the variable cost is $197 per unit, so each unit contributes 180 toward the fixed costs of $221k per year; at the current volume, that contribution covers the fixed costs several times over. The case does not turn on small movements in any of its figures: the price, the variable cost, or the fixed costs would each have to move a long way before the tier approached the volume at which it stops covering its costs. The margin of safety is the distance between the two volumes. The tier could lose most of its current volume and still cover its costs at the stated price and cost figures, and sales effort spent defending the last part of the volume is not what keeps the tier solvent. The figures are last year's actuals, and they describe the tier as it performed, not as it will perform. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and that gap bounds what the break-even figure can support: it shows where the current price stands against the current cost base, and it cannot show what a different price would do, because the volume response to a price change is the missing term in the case. On the stated figures the tier is not a break-even risk; the open question is the price itself, which this case does not test.
